rationale: A wins because it polices its own premises instead of selling them back to the founder as finished stories. "$550 per flight: the savings number Going's paid tier rests on" is useful because it admits the peg is "Honestly soft" and demands methodology; B's "From Scott's Cheap Flights to Going to AI trip planner: a deal-alert brand's long reinvention" tries to build a founder profile from one old brand name. B has usable raw material, but A would save you from walking into a reporter's first obvious question.
gaps_in_A: "Mistake fares vanish fast" is a strong consumer premise, but the update never says fares disappear quickly; it needs domain evidence or a named member example before it becomes more than inference.
"If the prevailing push in the space is toward agents that book end-to-end" is outside the supplied facts. A correctly caveats it, but the angle should stay parked until that external peg is sourced.
"Going bets the cheap-fare alert is only the top of the trip" may overstate company strategy unless Going confirms planning-before-booking is deliberate, not just launch sequencing.
gaps_in_B: "From Scott's Cheap Flights to Going to AI trip planner: a deal-alert brand's long reinvention" is the major offense. The update gives an old name, not a founder profile, rebrand narrative, milestone timeline, or "long reinvention."
"the prevailing model in AI travel tools is intent-first" imports a market thesis not in the update; prove it with current competitor coverage or cut the comparison.

"the core product — cheap-fare alerts — is free to ~2 million people" overstates the facts. The update says Going has ~2 million free members and a smaller paid base, not that the core alert product is simply free.
"tech business reporter covering SaaS subscription models" is the wrong shape for a consumer travel subscription. That is beat fog wearing a blazer.
